hints.hint: First write what each speaker was told: their own value plus the public number N. If the problem never settles what N measures, they were not told that either, so never run a separate case per option; that invents a fact and a fake contradiction. Work one seat at a time: for own value v, pool into ONE list every partner v allows across all options together (N minus v, N over v), dropping entries that break the domain rules. Its size decides all: one means that speaker knows, two or more means not, so v pinning the partner under one option alone rules nothing out. Save the first speaker's ignorance as a condition on their own value, then apply it where it bites: each partner in the second speaker's list IS the first speaker's value, so delete partners failing it and require two or more left. Answer with the own value passing this stronger test, never a tie-break on primality or looks.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts scored 0 (exec 149.358) and every one boxed the same wrong divisor 143; none hit the token cap, so this is a reasoning error, not looping. Shared path: open the sum reading and the product reading as separate self-contained cases, argue inside each that the holder of v plus that reading pins the partner, write impossible/contradiction (22-56 times in six rollouts), then abandon logic and pick the factor pair that merely looks special (two invoked primality). Not one rollout pooled the partners one private value admits across BOTH readings into a single list, and none carried the first speaker's ignorance onto the second speaker's partners. The incumbent says predicate abstractly and the model echoes the word without doing it, so the revision leads with the fact the failures violate - nobody was told which quantity N is - bans the per-option case split that manufactures the contradiction, and leaves only the pooled count and the prior-condition filter.

hints.hint: To find where ALL solutions lie, derive one necessary condition, not the solutions. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Only then nth-root that scalar: |z-a| = k|z-b| with k^n = |c|; write |c| as a prime power and divide its exponent by n. Square to clear moduli (z = x+iy). A zero x^2+y^2 coefficient means a line, else divide by it and complete the square for center and r > 0. Then STOP and answer: containment was all that was asked, so the condition need NOT be sufficient; listing solutions only invents contradictions. Never locate the center by imposing the distance condition on it, and never test the center against it. The center lies off the locus, so it must fail; that proves nothing.
hints.mutation: add-center-is-not-on-locus-guard (ban testing or re-deriving the center via the distance condition), replacing bare roots-of-unity ban
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts were correct (train saturated at 1.0), so the incumbent's cost is transfer and wasted budget, and both leaks trace to one confusion: treating the completed-square center as a point of the locus. Every rollout reached the modulus ratio and the right circle within ~1k tokens, then the four longest (5.2k-6.2k tokens, 4-29 'Wait' hedges) burned the rest on center confusion. One substituted the center into the ratio, saw it fail, concluded the circle was wrong, and re-derived individual solutions from a sixth-root/roots-of-unity branch (8 'unity' mentions). Another tried to LOCATE the center by imposing the distance condition on a candidate center on the real axis, produced two bogus centers, and oscillated between them and the correct algebra. The incumbent's stop rule bans enumerating roots but never says the center must violate the condition, so the revision adds that guard and keeps the necessity-suffices close.

hints.hint: Union = summed areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Frame on the covering shape's own edges: from the shared point P take its two edge directions as axes, so the cover is the wedge x >= 0, y >= 0. Audit that frame first: P is a corner, so stepping back from P along either axis must leave the cover. If every small step from P stays inside, you built P as a center; rebuild it. Then sign-test each vertex of the other shape S: covered iff both coordinates are >= 0. A negative coordinate kills containment; P inside S kills disjointness. Overlap is S clipped to the wedge; compute that area once in the easiest orientation and box the resulting union immediately. If rotating the wedge about P by its own angle carries each clipped piece onto the next, the pieces are congruent, overlap is angle-independent, and that union is maximal. No second orientation, no tangency.
hints.subagent_summary: 5/8. All 3 failures hit the 16384 cap. Two never built the corner frame: they offset P a full side in BOTH directions (-0.5..1.5 and -1.5..2.5), which makes P interior, so S looked wholly covered, overlap 1, and one boxed that union. The third did build the wedge and computed the correct clipped area and union by ~3.9k chars, then reopened the angle question and burned ~50k chars on rotated-square algebra (112 rotation mentions, 25 restatements of its own value) without ever closing. Winners reached the same first value and boxed it fast. The incumbent only forbids extending a full side both ways, but a bare ban loses to a concrete-looking offset. So the frame ban becomes an executable local test (P is a boundary point: a backward step must exit) and the anchor gets an immediate-box order so the first computed union is committed before any angle re-litigation.

hints.hint: A maximum count needs an upper bound plus a matching construction. With each term from any of N functions, one may serve many terms; it is pinned only where used, free elsewhere, so adjacent terms give no equation and its own consecutive values need not step by the common difference. Write the target as low-degree T(n); group indices by function used. On P's group, P - T vanishes but is not identically zero, since T cannot cancel P's leading term: at most d = deg P indices per group. Summing groups gives N x d, never N; expect far above N. Certify by substitution, not debate: give each function a block n_1..n_d, set P = T + c(x-n_1)...(x-n_d), c nonzero. Each n_j kills the factor: P(n_j) = T(n_j), P still degree d. Report N x d.
hints.subagent_summary: 8/8 with the incumbent, so the skeleton is sound; the diagnosis is budget, not aggregation. Every rollout still fought the same phantom obstruction on its way to the answer: 5 explicitly computed a single function's own successive difference, found it degree d-1 not constant, concluded 'must be linear', and only later recovered; 6 also called the product 'too high / seems too large' and reopened tightness. Token spend ran 8k-15k, and prior rounds show these same loops truncate when they start earlier. The incumbent only forbids chaining adjacent terms; it never says why one function may repeat, so the model re-derives that from scratch. This revision adds the one portable fact that settles it directly - a function is constrained only at the indices it served and free elsewhere, so its consecutive values need not step by the common difference - licenses reuse up front, and keeps the per-group cap, N x d aggregation, and the terminating substitution check.

hints.hint: Fit the parameters by exponentiating each given point alone (argument = base^height); check both. A vector equality is ONE constraint, a parallelogram: read (dx,dy) off it; midpoint or vertex-sum conditions only restate it. Carry one unknown, vertex (t,f(t)), closure f(t+dx)=f(t)+dy. The gap dy becomes ONE multiplicative factor on the argument. Never get that factor from log identities, where a base under 1 flips its direction. CALIBRATE it: the given pair already realizes (dx,dy), so divide their two arguments; that ratio IS the factor. A given vertex's x must then be a root, since the coincident vertex fits everything; divide it out, the rest is linear. No real root means an inverted factor, not a bad problem. Verify each height forward: base^height must give the argument. Area = |cross product|.
hints.subagent_summary: 5/8 correct; all 3 failures hit the 16384-token cap on the SAME step, the argument factor, not on the steps the incumbent guards. Two combined the two curve equations with log identities and treated log_{1/2}2 as +1, so the factor came out inverted (divide instead of multiply); one got discriminant -92, the other x^2=-5/3. The third slipped the parameter fit, self-corrected, then dropped dy entirely and equated the two arguments, getting 1/3=-7/3. None then applied the incumbent's degenerate-root test, because with no real root there was nothing to test; all three instead declared the problem contradictory and manufactured equal-diagonal-midpoint conditions (3, 6 and 14 mentions) until the cap. So the revision removes the identity step: calibrate the factor numerically from the given pair, which already realizes (dx,dy), and route any impossible root to the factor rather than to the problem.

hints.hint:
An answer counts only if it appears as an explicit product with one factor per move. Never reach for a remembered exponent: 1/n, 1/n!, 1/2^n and favourable-over-total are all wrong here, since reachable end states are few and unequally weighted, so the exponent must be counted off marked steps, not recognised.

Fix orientation once: a pile's bottom is its first arrival, its top its last. A named final position is thus a claim about arrival rank; bottom means it arrives first of all.

Then write out one complete move order realising the event and walk it, pricing each move from the current pile contents: weight 1 when only one pile can be drawn from, weight 1/2 when both can. Every item starting above your target must be moved aside first, and each of those is its own priced step. Multiply along the order, then add the qualifying orders.
hints.subagent_summary: 1/8 (idx 6, and it reached the graded value by dividing 1 by 8 sequences, not by pricing steps). Not one of the 8 rollouts ever wrote down a single concrete move order with per-step legality; all reasoned in prose then jumped to a remembered exponent. Part a came out as 1/24 (idx 0,2), 1/8 (idx 1,3), 1/16 (idx 4,7), 1/256 (idx 5) with totals variously guessed as 4!, 2^3, 2^4, 2^8. Six (idx 0,1,2,3,4,5,7 minus 6) then answered the graded part from uniformity: each item equally likely to be last, or a random permutation. So the incumbent's bans on 1/n and its run-of-halves warning are read past because the pricing walk is never started. This revision makes the move-by-move product the required deliverable, keeps arrival-rank orientation and the both-piles-drawable freeness test, and says the exponent must be counted, never recalled.

hints.hint:
Huge stated size, one entry asked: never do algebra at that size, and never carry it as a symbol. Get the law from small cases in exact numbers.
Fix the toy once by count-matching: n unknowns, n conditions, index range 1..n, the nonzero right-hand side last. Never renegotiate it; a toy is never inconsistent.
Solve toys cheaply: subtract each condition from the next to eliminate an unknown, repeat until one remains, then back-substitute. That is short enough to reach n=4, and two cases can never separate factorial from power growth.
Answer-first budget rule: as soon as a candidate law fits your cases, substitute the stated size and write that answer down. Only then test it further and revise. Never finish with no answer stated, and never redo a case you checked.
Ratios of consecutive answers name growth and sign; a computed case outranks any formula.
hints.subagent_summary: 0/8 (this same hint scored 5/8 in r14, so the ladder is fragile, not absent). Six rollouts hit the 16384-token cap having never written any answer; only two terminated, and both fit a law from n=2,3 alone (one shipped 1/2005, one declared even/odd cases exceptional). Only 3 of 8 ever reached n=4: rollouts burned hundreds of lines re-litigating n=2 and n=3 (36 mentions each) and then left numbers to expand (x-1)(x-2)... at the stated size chasing its x-coefficient (81-152 coefficient-of-x mentions, 44-100 of 2004!) or to introduce harmonic sums. The incumbent already orders n=2,3,4 and bans symbolic work at the stated size, but supplies no cheap way to solve a toy and no deadline, so the budget dies before n=4 and before any answer exists. This revision gives a concrete cheap elimination (consecutive differences), says outright that two cases cannot separate growth families, and adds an answer-first rule: state an answer as soon as a law fits, then refine.

hints.hint: Let N be the unstated count of identical units; recover it from arithmetic, not from the story. If every per-unit share must be whole, N divides each listed total, so admissible N are their common divisors: keep only divisors inside any stated bound on the count, otherwise take the largest, their gcd. When the story counts groups (streets, rows, batches), N = groups x units-per-group, so a group count is never N by itself even if every total divides by it, and never settle a tie by which story sounds more natural. Decide once whether each figure is an aggregate or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Divide each component by N, sum the shares, and apply any markup or discount as one factor. Before answering, substitute your numbers back: check every stated condition holds and none is left idle, every share is whole, and you report the quantity actually asked for.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 public rollouts scored 7/8 (train_i 0.875). The seven winners follow the incumbent cleanly: common divisors of the four listed totals, take the gcd, split, apply the markup. The single failure (longest run, ~15.5k tokens) also derives the full divisor list and the gcd, but then spends most of its length re-litigating whether the listed figures are aggregates or per-house amounts (chasing absurd counts), and at the very end downgrades N from the gcd to the group count, explicitly justifying it as the 'most reasonable' story reading and declaring both candidates valid. So the loss is not arithmetic but an endgame tie-break by narrative plausibility onto a number lifted from the text. I kept the incumbent's divisor core and bounded-count branch, banned the plausibility tie-break, and replaced the passive integrality check with substitute-back verification that every stated condition is satisfied and none left idle - a portable habit that should also help unrelated held-out items.

hints.hint: For p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with equal degrees n, skip the degree-n^2 coefficient grind. Find a common fixed point r and conjugate to it: set y=x-r, P(y)=p(r+y)-r, Q(y)=q(r+y)-r. Then P=Ay^n, Q=By^n are monomials and composing is mechanical: P(Q(y))=A(By^n)^n=AB^n y^(n^2), raising the inner value, not the outer coefficient. The origin is the center by construction; do not hunt another. Matching gives AB^n=BA^n; factor as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0, keeping both branches since B=A forces p=q. The identity is then automatic - expect that, not underdetermination; match free parameters to independent conditions and combine those symmetrically: add to pin one, subtract for the other. Answer in y.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts correct (4.1k-9.1k tokens, none truncated), so training is saturated and every point is transfer. Two wastes recur. (1) The 9.1k outlier (2x median) mis-nested the composition, substituting the already-cubed offset again to get BA^9, hence B^2=A^8 and B=+-A^4 (81 A^4 mentions); it then ratioed the two given conditions into a high-degree equation in the center and burned half its output trial-substituting integers. (2) All 8 rollouts re-hunt the center: 7-31 'fixed point' and 5-10 'another' mentions, mostly after the answer was already verified. Rounds 9/10 (exponent audits), 14/15 (factoring rules), 16 (no-ratio) and 17 (validate-against-p=q) all added corrective wording and all lost heldout. So instead of another audit this revision changes the representation: an explicit y=x-r conjugation turns both maps into monomials Ay^n, so composition is one syntactic step that cannot be mis-nested and the origin is the center by construction, ending the hunt.

hints.hint: For "how many repeats restore the original" problems, trace; don't theorize. One repeat = ALL listed sub-steps in order, each acting on what the previous produced. Count only COMPLETED repeats; numbering lines per sub-step inflates the count. Per sub-step rewrite the whole labeled state: concatenate the named blocks in the other order, copy the rest verbatim. A length-L block swap is L parallel slot-swaps, not one transposition, and overlapping sub-steps don't commute, so never claim order 2 untraced. Get each size's count by following ONE slot until it returns; no orbit exceeds the slot count, so a larger answer needs an lcm of traced orbits. From three real (size, count) pairs fit ONE formula growing with size, then substitute it back into the SMALLEST pair. A mismatch by one factor means your exponent is off by one; no size is exceptional and no answer is piecewise.
hints.subagent_summary: 4/8 correct. Failures never traced a full repeat. idx0 and idx4 read cycle type off sub-step shapes ('n transpositions, so order 2'), got counts that SHRANK with size, then answered piecewise or excused n=1 as special. idx7 fit a formula while writing that it contradicts its own smallest count, calling that acceptable. idx6 numbered every sub-step as a separate application, so its per-size counts were inflated by the sub-step count and it fit a doubled exponent (2^{2n-1}); idx4/idx7 landed one exponent off. Correct rollouts all followed one slot's orbit under whole repeats and got one growth law. So the revision adds: count only completed repeats (the inflation signature the incumbent misses), an orbit-length ceiling (no orbit exceeds the slot count) that kills invented large counts, and refit-against-the-smallest-pair with an off-by-one-exponent nudge instead of vague minimality.
